claims.statement: Misreading of p-values is common enough in published quantitative work that a national statistical association issued a formal statement of principles on their interpretation, and methodologists have catalogued the specific misreadings as a numbered list of errors with corrections.
claims.scope: The existence and motivation of these two published responses to p-value misinterpretation in the research literature. The lesson does not claim any particular prevalence rate, nor that any named group of clinicians makes these errors at a measured frequency.
claims.uncertainty: Neither source measures how often the errors occur; both describe them as common enough to warrant correction. The five readings in the opening scene are invented dialogue, not survey data.

claims.statement: In this framework a null hypothesis and an alternative hypothesis are two competing statements about the distribution behind the observed data; the null fixes the targeted quantity at one specified value, most often zero effect, and the alternative covers the remaining values.
claims.scope: The definitional framing of null and alternative hypotheses for a two-group comparison of means at introductory level. The lesson does not develop the measure-theoretic treatment, simple versus compound hypotheses, or optimality of tests.
claims.uncertainty: The convention of placing the null at zero is a convention rather than a requirement; the lesson states this and gives a non-zero null as a legitimate alternative in a retrieval item.

claims.statement: A p-value is computed on the assumption that every assumption in the statistical model holds, including the tested hypothesis, so the resulting probability bears on the whole model rather than on the tested hypothesis alone, and a small value indicates incompatibility between the data and that specified model without identifying which assumption failed.
claims.scope: The logical status of the assumptions behind any p-value from a conventional frequentist test. The lesson lists the assumptions relevant to the invented two-group comparison it uses and does not attempt a general taxonomy of model assumptions.
claims.uncertainty: Which assumption is responsible for a small p-value is not determinable from the p-value itself; the lesson states this limit explicitly rather than resolving it.

claims.statement: A test statistic is a function of the observed data chosen to measure the distance between the data and what the model predicts, taking values that grow as the data depart from the hypothesis being tested.
claims.scope: The general role of a test statistic, applied in this lesson to the specific case of an observed difference divided by its standard error. The lesson does not derive the sampling distribution of that statistic or treat other statistic families beyond naming them.

claims.statement: A p-value is the probability, computed under the assumption that every model assumption including the tested hypothesis is correct, that the chosen test statistic would be at least as extreme as the value actually observed.
claims.scope: The definition of a p-value for a conventional frequentist test, applied here to a two-sided test of a difference between two means and, in the transfer scene, to a difference between two proportions.
claims.uncertainty: The two-mean examples compute tail areas and matching intervals with a declared large-sample normal approximation using an estimated standard error. The lesson states openly that a pooled t reference with 58 degrees of freedom returns about 0.033 for the dinner-timing data instead of the normal-approximation value 0.029. The two-proportion transfer names its separate Wald approximation and its sparse-count limitation.

claims.statement: For two independent sample proportions, the unpooled Wald normal approximation estimates the standard error of their difference from the two observed proportions, uses a normal reference for the standardized difference, and can produce interval coverage below its nominal level.
claims.scope: The named procedure and its limitations in the invented transfer audit. The same unpooled estimated standard error is used for the displayed z statistic and 95 per cent interval so that the example is internally consistent. This lesson does not recommend a clinical-analysis method.
claims.uncertainty: Only five infections occur in the new-protocol arm, so the normal approximation is fragile and its nominal 95 per cent coverage is not assured. The example teaches interpretation of a reported result; selecting a sparse-count procedure for a real audit is outside scope.

claims.statement: The values of an effect whose tests return p above 0.05 form the corresponding 95 per cent confidence interval, so an interval excluding a hypothesised value and a test of that value returning p below 0.05 are one result expressed in two notations and cannot disagree.
claims.scope: The correspondence between an interval at a stated level and the set of hypothesised values not rejected at the matching cut-off, for the standard two-sided case used throughout this lesson.
claims.uncertainty: The correspondence holds when interval and test are built from the same model, estimate, standard error, and reference curve, which is the case for every worked example here. Intervals constructed by other methods need not correspond exactly to a given test.

claims.statement: A p-value is not the probability that the tested hypothesis is true, and its complement is not the probability that an effect is real; the p-value assumes the tested hypothesis rather than assigning it a probability, so reading it as a hypothesis probability inverts the conditional.
claims.scope: The interpretation of p-values produced by conventional frequentist tests. The lesson does not develop the Bayesian machinery that would be required to obtain a probability for a hypothesis, and refers the conditional-inversion reasoning back to PREM-STA-004.

claims.statement: A p-value is not the probability that the observed result was produced by chance alone, because chance acting alone is among the assumptions used to compute it, and a probability deduced from a set of assumptions cannot also be the probability that those assumptions hold.
claims.scope: The interpretation of a p-value computed under a null model in which sampling variation is the only source of the observed departure.

claims.statement: A p-value, and the statistical significance derived from it, does not measure the size of an effect or the importance of a result, because the statistic behind it combines the size of the effect with the precision of the estimate and cannot be decomposed back into them.
claims.scope: The relationship between a p-value, the effect size, and the precision of an estimate. The lesson demonstrates the point with invented paired studies and stops short of judging whether any particular effect size matters clinically, which is deferred to PREM-STA-012.

claims.statement: A p-value above the conventional cut-off does not demonstrate that there is no effect, because the tested value is then only one among many values compatible with the data, and the observed estimate remains the value most compatible with them.
claims.scope: The interpretation of a result falling above a chosen cut-off. The lesson establishes what such a result fails to show and refers the separate question of what a study of a given size could have detected to PREM-STA-009.

claims.statement: The cut-off of 0.05 is a conventional choice rather than a result of the arithmetic, and scientific or policy conclusions should not be based only on whether a p-value passes a specified threshold.
claims.scope: The status of the 0.05 convention in reporting and decision-making. The lesson supports the point with its own arithmetic showing that the reference curve chosen moves the computed value from 0.029 to about 0.033 for identical data.
claims.uncertainty: The 0.029 against 0.033 comparison is this lesson's own computation on invented data and is offered as an illustration of sensitivity, not as a sourced general result about the size of such discrepancies.

claims.statement: The significance level alpha is a probability fixed in advance as part of a study's design, while the p-value is computed from the data after they arrive; the two are compared but are distinct quantities.
claims.scope: The definitional separation of a pre-specified cut-off from a data-dependent p-value. The lesson deliberately stops before developing alpha as a long-run error rate, which belongs to PREM-STA-009.

claims.statement: Statistical significance is a dichotomous description of where a p-value fell relative to a chosen cut-off, and so is a property of the result of a statistical test rather than a property of the effect or the population being studied.
claims.scope: The referent of the technical phrase statistically significant. The lesson uses this to separate the technical sense from the everyday sense of the word and hands the full separation of statistical from practical importance to PREM-STA-012.

terms.definition: A statement fixing the quantity under study at one specified value, adopted so that a model can predict what data should look like if it held. In this lesson it sets the true difference in mean fasting glucose between the late and early dinner groups at 0 mg/dL. It is adopted as a starting assumption for calculation and carries no suggestion that anyone believes it.

alignment.note: PREM-SCI-002 defines a hypothesis as a proposed explanation or relationship from which observable expectations can be derived. A null hypothesis is one of those, narrowed in two ways: it must fix a numerical quantity at a single stated value, and it is adopted for the purpose of being tested against rather than because it is the explanation on offer. The scientific hypothesis in the dinner-timing study is that later dinners raise fasting glucose; the null hypothesis is its numerical foil, and scene 2 bridges the two senses where the word first appears in the new sense.

terms.definition: The statement covering the values the null hypothesis excludes. A two-sided alternative allows the quantity to differ from the null value in either direction, which is the form used throughout this lesson; a one-sided alternative allows departure in one direction only and counts the other direction as no evidence at all.

alignment.note: Narrows PREM-SCI-002's general sense of a hypothesis to the specific complementary statement paired with a null in a statistical test. It is defined by what the null leaves out rather than by an explanatory account of its own, so it is a weaker object than the scientific hypothesis PREM-SCI-002 teaches.

terms.definition: The full set of assumptions needed to turn a hypothesis into a prediction about data. For the dinner-timing comparison it holds the null value, the treatment of participants as independent contributors, the within-group spread of 16 mg/dL, the shape of the reference curve, and the assumption that the analysis reported was the analysis planned. Every probability in this lesson is computed inside this set, so it inherits every fault the set contains.

alignment.note: PREM-SCI-010 defines a scientific model as a selective representation of a system built to answer a stated question, and PREM-SCI-010's term-model-assumption as a simplification accepted so the model can represent selected relationships. This lesson narrows both to the statistical case: the representation is of how data would be generated under a stated hypothesis, and its assumptions are the specific conditions a test's probability calculation relies on. The narrower sense does not replace the broader one, and the assumptions here are model assumptions in exactly PREM-SCI-010's sense.

terms.definition: A number computed from the data to measure how far the observation sits from what the model predicts, built so that it grows as the data depart from the hypothesis. In this lesson it is the observed difference minus the null value, divided by the standard error, which expresses the gap in standard errors and so removes the original units. The two-mean worked examples label it z because they use a declared normal approximation; another procedure may use a different reference curve and label.

The distribution of results the null model predicts across repeats of the study. For the dinner-timing difference this lesson uses a normal approximation centred on 0 mg/dL with an estimated standard error of 4.13 mg/dL. A p-value is an area measured on the selected distribution, which is why the shape of the curve is itself a modelling assumption.

The probability, computed on the assumption that the null hypothesis and every other assumption in the statistical model are correct, that the test statistic would be at least as extreme as the value actually observed. For the dinner-timing study the two-sided normal-approximation value is 0.029. It is a statement about data made under an assumption about the world, and it reports neither the probability that the null is true, nor the probability that chance produced the result, nor the size of any effect.

A probability chosen before the data are seen, setting how far into the tail of the null distribution a result must fall before the analysis calls the data incompatible with the null. It belongs to the study's design and is conventionally 0.05. It is compared with the p-value and is a separate quantity from it, since one is fixed in advance and the other is measured afterwards.

A label applied to a test result whose p-value falls at or below the significance level chosen in advance. It records where one number landed relative to a threshold. In this technical sense the word carries no information about how large an effect is, how important it is, or whether anyone should act on it, which separates it sharply from the everyday sense of significant meaning sizeable or worth attention.

The reasoning error of treating the probability of A given B as though it were the probability of B given A. Applied to a test result it turns a probability computed under a hypothesis into a probability of that hypothesis, so that p = 0.029 is misread as a 2.9 per cent chance the null is true or a 97.1 per cent chance the effect is real.

alignment.note: Adopts PREM-STA-004's meaning without change: treating P(A given B) as though it were P(B given A). That lesson established the error with screening tables, where the same test gave 0.269 in one clinic and 0.818 in another while its detection rate stayed fixed. This lesson applies the identical error to a p-value, which is the case PREM-STA-004 explicitly forwarded here, and adds no new sense of the term.

One arithmetic point deserves explicit record because it affects how a reviewer should read the pack. The block's canonical p = 0.029 and its canonical interval are both computed with a declared large-sample normal approximation, which is what the block's use of the 1.96 multiplier implies. The worked statistic is therefore labelled z, not t. Because the standard error is estimated, a pooled Student t procedure is a defensible alternative; with 58 degrees of freedom it returns about 0.033 for the same data. The pack states this openly in scene 3 and uses it in scene 5 as evidence that the 0.05 convention cannot bear the weight often placed on it.

site/data/premed-terminology.json was read before the glossary was designed. Nine terms are defined here. Four carry an alignment block:

  • null hypothesis — relation narrow, prior lesson PREM-SCI-002, which owns hypothesis as a proposed explanation yielding observable expectations. A null hypothesis narrows that to a numerical statement fixed at one value and adopted in order to be tested against. Scene 2 bridges the two senses where the word first appears in the new sense.
  • alternative hypothesis — relation narrow, prior lesson PREM-SCI-002, for the same reason; it is defined by what the null excludes rather than by an explanatory account of its own.
